MVP LLM Product Management What to cut from an AI MVP’s first release in 2026 Irina B 9 min read · Oct 4, 2026 -- 1 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size You have an LLM feature, a fixed runway, and a roadmap that gets longer every week. The fastest way to spend that runway is to launch an AI MVP that tries to prove five things at once. A first release should prove one AI job, end to end, with real users. Everything else can wait. This article is about telling the two apart. It usually starts in a planning session that goes a little too well. Someone suggests letting users pick between models. Someone else wants an admin console for enterprise buyers. Then came a usage dashboard, prompt settings for power users, and a second model “just in case.” Every idea sounds reasonable. With modern LLM APIs, every idea also looks like it would take about a week. That’s the trap. A week of work at a time is how a focused first release turns into a half-finished platform. Why LLM MVPs grow faster than their runway Feature creep isn’t new, but products built on large language models are especially vulnerable to it. Three things make it worse. Demos are cheap. Products aren’t. You can build a convincing LLM demo in an afternoon. The version that handles messy real input, fails gracefully, and behaves consistently enough for customers to rely on takes far longer. When every idea looks like a quick demo, teams underestimate what it takes to ship each one properly. Every AI feature adds uncertainty. A traditional feature either works or it doesn’t. An LLM feature works most of the time, in ways that vary from one input to the next. Each additional AI feature is another unpredictable behavior to test, explain, and support. Two AI features aren’t twice the work. They’re two sources of doubt about why users stay or leave. The tooling invites options. LLM platforms come with knobs: model versions, parameters, system prompts, providers. It feels natural to expose them. But every option you expose is a promise you have to test, document, and keep. The result is a first release that’s broad and shallow. Users can’t tell what it’s for, and your team can’t tell which part is working. The one job your AI MVP must prove Before you cut anything, you need something to measure features against. That’s the one job: the single task your AI feature has to complete, end to end, for one type of user. “End to end” matters here. It means the whole loop works in real conditions: A real user brings real input. The model produces an output. The user decides what to do with it: accept, edit, or reject. The result lands where it needs to go, and you can see what happened. If any step in that loop is missing, you haven’t proven the job. You’ve proven a demo. To make this concrete, imagine a B2B software company adding an LLM feature to its customer support tool. The original wish list includes drafting replies to tickets, summarizing long threads, detecting customer sentiment, suggesting help articles, routing tickets to the right team, and a dashboard showing how much time the AI saved. The team’s first step is to write down the one job in a single sentence. For this product, it could read like this: One-job statement: When a new support ticket arrives, the AI prepares a first reply that the agent can check, adjust, and send, so no one starts from a blank box. Once that sentence exists, most of the wishlist moves to “later” on its own. Summaries, sentiment detection, routing, and the time-saved dashboard might all be valuable one day. None of them is needed to prove that drafted replies help agents. A useful test for any feature: if it disappeared, would the one job still work end to end? If the answer is yes, it’s a candidate for cutting. Marc Caposino, Co-Founder & Chief Creative Director at Fuselab Creative, uses an even simpler filter when founders bring him a long feature list: “When a founder shows me twelve AI features, I ask one question: which of these would you bet the company on? That’s your first release. The other eleven are a conversation after real users have touched the first one.” Press enter or click to view image in full size A conversational AI workspace designed by Fuselab Creative: one question, one answer, one clear job Defining the one job is also the best way to protect your AI MVP scope later. When someone proposes a new feature mid-build, you don’t debate whether it’s a good idea. You ask whether the one job needs it. If you’d like a refresher on what an MVP is supposed to do in the first place, we cover the fundamentals in our guide to what an MVP is . What to cut from the first release Four items quietly expand the scope of almost every LLM MVP. None of them helps prove the one job, and all of them are easier to add later than to maintain early. Model settings Temperature sliders, model pickers, custom system prompts, and “creativity” controls feel like features. For most users, they’re homework. They also multiply your testing surface: every setting creates combinations of behavior you have to check and support. Instead: choose one configuration that works well for the one job, and tune it yourself based on what you see in the logs. Bring it back when: several different customers ask for the same control, and you can explain in one sentence what it’s for.
